passage:
Counselling note, Tuesday afternoon.
Kunal arrived fifteen minutes early and sat with his bag held tight on his knees. He said his father called him "ungrateful" on the phone last night, only because Kunal asked whether he really had to take over the family printing press after his degree. He kept repeating, "They built everything for me." His voice dropped when he said none of his hostel friends get it; their parents "just want them to have any job." He showed me a notebook of stage-set sketches he has never shown at home. I did not tell him what to choose. I asked which parts of the press he actually likes. He said the smell of ink and the late-night rush with his uncle before an election. Midway, his elder sister Bidisha texted: "Papa is hurt, not angry. Come home Sunday?" He smiled for the first time. Before our next meeting he will write two lists: what he wants, and what he was handed.

qa.q: What did Kunal's father call him on the phone last night?
qa.a: His father called him "ungrateful".

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling when he keeps repeating "They built everything for me"?
qa.a: He seems guilty, as if asking about his own future betrays his family's work, and lonely, because his hostel friends don't understand.

qa.q: How does the counsellor's two-list task help Kunal sort out his choice?
qa.a: It lets him separate what he truly wants from what he was handed, without anyone telling him which to pick, so he can keep the parts of the press he likes.

qa.q: How does Bidisha seem to read the fight between Kunal and their father?
qa.a: Bidisha sees their father as hurt rather than angry, and she tries to keep Kunal connected by inviting him home on Sunday.

grounding: A young adult is called ungrateful for questioning the family career and feels guilt and loneliness while working out what is really his.

passage:
Sunday, late.
Pradeep bhaiya laughed at dinner and said I've "got lost in hostel life." All because I said I wasn't sure I'd keep the Tuesday fast this year. Mummy went quiet and cleared the plates without looking at me. Nobody said ungrateful, but it sat on the table anyway.
I'm not saying the fast is wrong. I kept it for nine years. I loved the quiet mornings with Mummy, the temple bell on the walk back. I just want to know if I do it because I believe, or because it's what our house does.
Came up to the terrace after. Messaged three friends; all three sent memes back. Felt so alone up here, and so guilty for making Mummy's face go like that.
Tomorrow I'll ask her why she started fasting. Maybe her answer helps me find mine.
- Payal

qa.q: How many years has Payal kept the Tuesday fast?
qa.a: Payal kept the Tuesday fast for nine years.

qa.q: What does Payal feel up on the terrace after dinner, and why?
qa.a: Payal feels alone, because the friends only sent memes back, and guilty for upsetting Mummy, even though the question was honest.

qa.q: Why is asking Mummy why she started fasting a wise next step for Payal?
qa.a: It turns a tense silence into a real conversation, and hearing Mummy's reasons may help Payal tell apart belief that is personal from habit that was inherited.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she cleared the plates without looking at Payal?
qa.a: Mummy may have felt hurt or worried that a practice she shared with Payal was being rejected, and unsure how to respond in front of Pradeep.

grounding: A young adult who questions a family religious practice is called lost and feels guilt and loneliness while asking what belief is truly theirs.

passage: Sit, Jyoti, the chai will get cold. You asked how I knew. I didn't, not at first. At twenty-five I was a junior engineer at the textile mill because my father had been one, and his father before him. One monsoon evening I noticed I was only really happy on Saturdays, teaching the workers' children maths under the loading shed. I didn't resign. I asked the manager for one afternoon a week to run a training class for new apprentices. When Appa heard, he went quiet for two days. So I sat with him on the steps and said, "I still love the machines you taught me. I also love teaching. I want to find out how much of each is mine." Three years later I moved to the training college. He came to my first lecture in his good shirt. So when people say Sharmila left engineering, I tell them I carried it into the classroom.

qa.q: What did Sharmila ask the manager for?
qa.a: Sharmila asked for one afternoon a week to run a training class for new apprentices.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel on the Saturdays under the loading shed, and what showed it?
qa.a: Sharmila felt genuinely happy there, noticing that teaching the workers' children was the only time of the week that felt that way.

qa.q: Why was asking for one afternoon a week, instead of resigning, a wise turning point in the story?
qa.a: It tested teaching in a small, safe way, kept the engineering Sharmila valued, and gave Appa time to adjust instead of facing a sudden break.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt during the two quiet days, and what changed for him later?
qa.a: Appa may have felt hurt or afraid the family line was ending; after Sharmila explained with respect, he came to the first lecture in his good shirt, showing pride.

grounding: A young professional who followed the family engineering script tests teaching in small steps, keeps the parts Sharmila values, and explains the choice respectfully.

passage: The monsoon had flooded half the lane, and the Saturday market was thinner than usual. Payal stood under the dripping tarpaulin of the family snack stall, beside the pakora wok her mother Sudha had run for twenty years. Payal had fried pakoras every weekend since school, never once asking whether she wanted to. Last month, at twenty-four, she had asked for one corner of the counter to try her own baked millet cookies. Today only eleven people stopped, and rain smudged her handwritten labels. Sudha watched her dab the tray dry. "You don't like frying?" she asked, not looking up. Payal kept her voice gentle. "I like working with you, Ma. I like this stall. I want to see if baking is also mine. It's one corner, not a new shop." Sudha bought the last cookie herself, broke it in half, and chewed slowly.

qa.q: How many people stopped at Payal's corner today?
qa.a: Only eleven people stopped.

qa.q: What might Sudha be worried about when she asks "You don't like frying?" without looking up?
qa.a: Sudha may be anxious that Payal is rejecting the stall and their work together, and a little hurt that the old routine isn't enough.

qa.q: Which part of Payal's approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Payal kept the change small, one corner and not a new shop, and told Sudha what she valued, so the test felt like an addition rather than a rejection.

qa.q: What would change if Payal had quit the stall to open a bakery overnight?
qa.a: Sudha would likely feel abandoned and blamed, and Payal would lose the chance to learn slowly whether baking was truly hers.

grounding: A young adult who realises she followed a family routine tests one small change, keeps the parts she values, and explains it respectfully despite the rain.

passage: Siddharth's laptop still showed the sprint board when Vaibhav bhaiya walked into the Pune flat carrying two plates of misal. "You joined an urban-design course? On top of office?" Siddharth nodded. For three years he had written code because that was the family plan: engineering, campus job, then maybe onsite. Sometime last winter he noticed he spent lunch breaks sketching the crowded bus stops outside the tech park. So he signed up for one evening module, not a new degree. "I'm not quitting," he said. "I like the problem-solving you pushed me toward. I just want to find out if I like it for streets too." Vaibhav chewed slowly. "Papa will ask why." "Then I'll tell him what I kept and what I'm trying," Siddharth said. "He deserves the whole answer, not a surprise."

qa.q: What did Siddharth sketch during his lunch breaks?
qa.a: He sketched the crowded bus stops outside the tech park.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to feel when he says "I'm not quitting"?
qa.a: He seems calm but a little defensive, keen to reassure Vaibhav that he isn't rejecting the family plan.

qa.a: It lets him test a real interest without burning down his job, so he can find out what is his before making a bigger change.

qa.a: Vaibhav may be surprised and a little protective, worried how Papa will react, but he listens and doesn't argue.

passage: In the mud-walled courtyard, two-year-old Pooja tugs at Shalini maasi's dupatta. Maasi has rocked her through every fever and every scraped knee this winter. Pooja holds up a soggy piece of roti and pushes it toward Maasi's mouth, then waits. Maasi takes a tiny bite. "Mmm, thank you!" Pooja giggles, climbs into her lap and presses a sticky cheek to her arm. Then she wriggles down and runs to fetch her clay bullock to show her.

qa.q: What does Pooja fetch to show Shalini maasi?
qa.a: Pooja fetches her clay bullock.

qa.q: What does Pooja's pushing the roti toward Maasi suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Pooja feels safe and affectionate with Maasi, trusting enough to share her food and wait for a reaction.

qa.q: How does Maasi's small bite and "thank you" help Pooja?

passage: It is a hot Christmas afternoon in Valparaíso, and the fan hums over the tiles. Noa, not yet two, toddles to her papá, Diego, holding a dripping slice of watermelon in both fists. She pushes it at his chin. He pretends to take a huge bite. Noa squeals, drops the melon and reaches up with both arms. Diego lifts her. She tucks her head under his jaw, the way she does after every bad dream, then wriggles down to bring him her toy boat.

qa.q: What does Noa hold in both fists?
qa.a: Noa holds a dripping slice of watermelon in both fists.

qa.q: How can you tell that Noa feels safe with Diego?
qa.a: She reaches up with both arms and tucks her head under his jaw, the same way she does after bad dreams, which shows deep trust and comfort.

qa.q: Which response from Diego helps Noa, and why?
qa.a: His playful pretend bite and quick lift answer her gift and her reach, showing that her closeness is welcome.

passage:

Holi morning: drums boom in the lane. Leela runs straight to Mohit, burrows into his kurta, then offers him a crumb of her gujiya.
Two days later: the courtyard is quiet again. Leela drags her little toy drum over, bangs it once, and looks up at him, grinning.

passage:
Monday: Behind the school water tank, Francis, ten, whispered to Jahnavi that he still couldn't swim. "Best friends keep everything," she said, hooking her little finger into his.
Thursday: On the pool trip, Jahnavi giggled to two girls, "Francis needs armbands!" The whole bench turned. Francis stared at the wet tiles, throat tight, and didn't talk to anyone on the bus. That night he told his mother he never wanted a best friend again. She sat on his bed, listened to all of it, and said being hurt meant he had really trusted someone.
The next Tuesday: Jahnavi pushed a folded note onto his desk: "Sorry. I wanted them to laugh with me." Francis read it twice, then slid it into his pencil box, not ready to smile yet.

qa.q: What secret did Francis whisper to Jahnavi?
qa.a: Francis whispered that he still couldn't swim.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling on the bus after the pool trip?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and betrayed, so hurt that he later said he never wanted a best friend again.

qa.q: How did Francis's mother support him, and why did it help?
qa.a: She listened to all of it and told him the hurt showed he had really trusted someone, which helped him see trust as worth something, not foolish.

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi have told the secret, according to her note?
qa.a: Jahnavi wrote that she wanted the other girls to laugh with her, so she seems to have traded Francis's trust for a moment of belonging.

grounding: A child shares a secret with his one best friend, is devastated when she betrays it, and begins learning what trusting a single peer costs and means.

passage: Vikas, you're sulking because Monty told your secret? Let me tell you about Harish. When I was eleven, in Nashik, Harish was my one real friend. I told him I was scared of the dark and slept holding my mother's shawl. Nobody else knew. At the Ganesh festival he told the whole gully, and for a month they called me "shawl-boy." I cried behind the water tank where no one could see. I decided I would never trust anybody again. But that winter Harish came to our door with his kite and said sorry, badly, staring at his feet. I made him wait a week. Then we flew that kite together off the roof. So your Suraj-dada learnt early that a friend who hurts you can still be worth the risk.

qa.q: What did the gully call Suraj for a month?
qa.a: They called him "shawl-boy" for a month.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after Harish told the whole gully?
qa.a: Suraj felt devastated and ashamed, crying behind the water tank and deciding never to trust anybody again.

qa.q: Why was making Harish wait a week before flying the kite a sensible turning point in the story?
qa.a: It let Suraj take his hurt seriously while still leaving room for repair, so trust could return slowly instead of being cut off for good.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt standing at the door with his kite?
qa.a: Harish likely felt ashamed and nervous, which is why his apology came out badly while he stared at his feet.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing one best friend as a boy, sharing a secret, feeling devastated by the betrayal, and slowly learning to risk trust again.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof, PE was cancelled, and with the class teacher away at a meeting, Class 4B was stuck indoors with colouring sheets. Nandini sat beside Farida as always. Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths. Then, across the room, Rukhsar whispered loudly, "Farida says you're a finger-counter!" Nandini's crayon snapped. She stared at Farida, who went red and looked at the window. There was nowhere to go; the corridor was flooded. Nandini pressed her forehead to the desk so nobody would see her eyes. At home time Farida held out half her samosa without a word. Nandini didn't take it, but she didn't walk away either, and they waited for the rain side by side.

qa.q: What did only Farida know about Nandini?
qa.a: Only Farida knew that Nandini still counted on her fingers under the desk during maths.

qa.q: What does Nandini's snapped crayon and hidden face suggest she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she felt shocked, betrayed and embarrassed, trying to hide tears from the class.

qa.q: What could Farida try next, beyond offering the samosa?
qa.a: Farida could say sorry out loud and admit she told the secret, which would show Nandini she understands the hurt, not just want it to pass.

qa.q: What was it like for Farida when Nandini stared at her?
qa.a: Farida likely felt guilty and ashamed, turning red and looking away because she knew she had broken her best friend's trust.

passage: Every photo Vera posted from Lyon looked the same: perfect croissant, perfect bike ride, a caption with three sparkles. Two hundred likes, forty comments. At lunch the table laughed at her jokes, and she laughed with them, and walked home alone. Nobody knew she had failed the chemistry mock twice or that she lay awake doubting she'd get into any programme at all. Telling felt risky, like people would see the cracks and leave. On Friday the tram broke down, and she ended up waiting beside Tariq, the quiet boy from physics. "You always look like you've got it sorted," he said. Vera almost laughed it off. Instead she heard herself say, "I failed chem. Twice." Tariq blinked. "Same. Well, maths." They talked for forty minutes, and it was the first time in months her chest felt loose.

qa.q: How many times did Vera fail the chemistry mock?
qa.a: She failed the chemistry mock twice.

qa.q: Why was Vera afraid to tell anyone about her doubts?
qa.a: She feared that if people saw the cracks, they would leave, so she felt safer hiding behind a perfect image even though it left her lonely.

qa.q: What small step helped Vera feel less alone?
qa.a: Choosing to answer Tariq honestly instead of laughing it off opened a real conversation, showing that one true disclosure can start closeness.

qa.q: How might Tariq have seen Vera before and after the tram stop?
qa.a: Before, Tariq saw someone who looked sorted and out of reach; afterwards he likely felt relieved to learn she struggled too, just as he did.

grounding: A teenager who shows a polished self and hides doubts feels alone among many, until a real disclosure begins to change that.

passage: The robotics lab at Kendriya School smelled of solder and old chalk. Gopika was team lead, the girl who always knew the answer, whose reels of the line-follower bot got shared by juniors. Nobody saw her rewire the same board at eleven at night, sure she was a fraud who'd been lucky. At lunch she sat with six people and felt like she was behind glass. On Wednesday the bot died again two days before the district round. Hemant, who handled the code, found her staring at it. "Should I tell Sir we're behind?" he asked. Gopika's throat tightened. "Hemant, I don't actually know what's wrong. I haven't for a week." He put down his laptop. "I thought I was the only one faking it." They laughed shakily, pulled up a stool each, and started over from the battery.

qa.q: How many days before the district round did the bot die again?
qa.a: The bot died again two days before the district round.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling at lunch, sitting with six people?
qa.a: Gopika felt lonely and cut off, as if she were behind glass, because nobody knew her doubts.

qa.q: What went right when Gopika told Hemant the truth?
qa.a: Her honesty let Hemant admit his own doubts, so they could work on the real problem together instead of both pretending.

qa.q: How did Gopika's confession affect Hemant?
qa.a: Hemant seemed relieved, because he had thought he was the only one faking it and now felt less alone.

grounding: A teenager keeps up a polished, capable image while hiding doubts, feels alone among many, and a real disclosure begins to ease it.

passage:
Hi Pankaj bhaiya,
You asked on the phone why I sounded weird. I didn't answer, so I'm writing instead.
You've seen my page: dance videos, lots of friends, everything bright. I have 900 followers and a class full of people who say "Nikita is so fun." But I have never told any of them that I cry before tests, or that I don't know what I want to study. I'm scared if they see the real me, they'll think I'm boring and drift off. So I keep smiling, and I feel alone in a crowd every single day.
Last week I told one girl, Simran, that I was nervous about boards. She said she was too. We walked home together instead of scrolling. It felt small but real.
Can I call you on Sunday and just talk, without being fun?
Nikita

qa.q: How many followers does Nikita have?
qa.a: Nikita has 900 followers.

qa.q: What is Nikita afraid will happen if people see who Nikita really is?
qa.a: Nikita is afraid people will find the real Nikita boring and drift off, which is why the smiling continues even though Nikita feels alone in a crowd.

qa.a: One honest sentence got an honest reply and a walk home together, so small, real disclosures to a few people may help more than a bright page.

passage:
Dear Anjali,
It's been almost a year, and I'm sorry it took me this long to write.
When I started seeing Rohit, I let everything else slide. I skipped our Sunday badminton, then stopped replying to the group, then missed your birthday dinner because he wanted a quiet evening. I told myself that's what being close meant: always there, always yes.
Last month he asked what I wanted for my birthday and I couldn't answer. I didn't know what I even liked anymore. That scared me more than any fight.
I'm not leaving him. I love him. But I've signed up for badminton again, Saturdays, and I've told him that's my morning.
I miss you. I miss who I was with you. Would you play a match with me, if you still want to?
Love,
Charu

qa.q: Which day is Charu's new badminton?
qa.a: Charu has signed up for badminton on Saturdays.

qa.q: Why did Charu feel scared when Rohit asked about her birthday?
qa.a: Charu was frightened to realise that nothing felt like a clear personal wish anymore, which showed how much of Charu's own self had disappeared into the relationship.

qa.q: What is Charu's letter doing well as a repair?
qa.a: It owns the specific ways Charu let Anjali down, gives a concrete step, and invites Anjali back without pressure, so Anjali can choose.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel reading this letter after almost a year?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a mix of hurt from being dropped and warmth at being missed, and could need time before saying yes to a match.

grounding: A young adult in a first serious relationship notices having dropped friends and interests to be close, and starts reclaiming a self that can stay whole.

passage: So you want to know why Sunaina almost left? Honestly, it was me. I'm Sarika, I'm twenty-one, and when we started dating I kept everything on a timer. Two dinners a week, never at my flat, never with my friends. She'd ask about my family and I'd change the topic. I told myself I was keeping my independence. Really I was scared that if she saw all of me, she'd go, and I'd be the one left standing. Then one night she said, very quietly, "I feel like I'm dating your calendar." That hit. I didn't fix it overnight. I brought her to my friend's birthday. I told her about my parents' divorce, badly, crying into a plate of momos. I still keep my Friday evenings for painting. But now she knows what's in the paintings.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say that hit Sarika?
qa.a: Sunaina said, "I feel like I'm dating your calendar."

qa.q: What was Sarika really afraid of when keeping Sunaina at a distance?
qa.a: Sarika was afraid Sunaina would leave after seeing everything, so the distance was protection against being hurt, not true independence.

qa.q: Which of Sarika's changes shows a healthy balance, and why?
qa.a: Keeping Friday painting while sharing its meaning with Sunaina shows Sarika can stay herself and still let Sunaina close.

qa.q: How might the arm's-length rules have felt for Sunaina?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt shut out and lonely inside the relationship, as if she was scheduled rather than wanted.

grounding: A young adult in a first serious relationship keeps a partner at arm's length for safety and learns that closeness needs a self that can open while staying whole.

passage:
Week one: Mehak cancels her Thursday pottery class because Kishore finishes work early on Thursdays. "It's just one class," she tells her flatmate, and spends the evening watching him play video games.
Week five: The unfinished bowl sits dusty on her shelf. Her college friends have made a group plan without asking her. Mehak scrolls through their photos at midnight, a little hollow, wondering when she last did anything that was only hers.
Week eight: She's back at the wheel, clay up to her wrists. Kishore picks her up after class and asks to see the new mug. On the drive home she tells him she also wants one weekend a month with her friends. He's quiet, then says, "Okay. I didn't realise you'd stopped." Mehak squeezes his hand, relieved and still hers.

qa.a: She cancelled it because Kishore finishes work early on Thursdays.

qa.q: What could Mehak's week-eight choices teach someone in a first serious relationship?
qa.a: Staying close does not mean giving up everything; returning to pottery and asking for time with friends kept the relationship and her self both alive.

passage: Rehana, you asked why I only have four names on speed dial. Come, sit. When I was twenty-five I had eight hundred contacts, three office groups, a party every Saturday. And I would come home and eat standing at the counter, feeling like nobody knew me at all. One night my mother's scan came back unclear, and I scrolled that whole list and couldn't think of one person to call. That frightened me more than the scan. So I chose. Three friends. A call every Sunday, even if it was only ten minutes. I made myself say true things, like "I'm not coping this week." Once Meenal and I fought about a wedding and didn't speak for a month. I rang her anyway, awkward as anything. We are still friends. Kashish didn't get less lonely with more people, beta. It happened with fewer, and more honest.

qa.q: How many contacts did Kashish have at twenty-five?
qa.a: Kashish had eight hundred contacts.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel on the night of the unclear scan, and why?
qa.a: Kashish was frightened to realise that, among so many contacts, there was not one person to call, which showed how lonely life had become.

qa.q: Why was ringing Meenal after a month of silence an important choice in the story?
qa.a: It showed Kashish tolerating awkward repair instead of letting a fight end the friendship, which is what kept that close tie alive.

qa.q: How might Meenal have felt when Kashish rang after the fight?
qa.a: Meenal may have felt surprised and relieved, and perhaps a little awkward too, but glad that Kashish cared enough to call first.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling lonely despite many contacts at twenty-five and easing that isolation by investing honestly in a few friends, including through awkward repair.

passage: The call dropped for the third time; the Bengaluru building's Wi-Fi was down again, and Yusuf was already four time zones away in Doha. Tanvir stood on the stairwell landing, the only spot with signal, phone pressed to his ear. They'd barely spoken in the six weeks since their fight about Tanvir missing Yusuf's engagement. Tanvir had a hundred people in his contacts who'd cheer his posts, and not one he'd told that he'd been eating dinner alone every night. When the line reconnected, the silence was thick. "I'm sorry I missed it," Tanvir said. "I was ashamed I couldn't afford the ticket, so I just went quiet. That was worse." Yusuf let out a breath. "You could've said that." "I'm saying it now. Can we do Sunday calls again? Even bad-signal ones?" Yusuf laughed, a little stiffly. "Stairwell Sundays, then."

qa.q: Where was the only spot with signal?
qa.a: The stairwell landing was the only spot with signal.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's confession suggest he had been feeling since the fight?
qa.a: It suggests Tanvir had been ashamed and lonely, hiding behind silence rather than admitting why he missed the engagement.

qa.q: What small step helps rebuild the friendship?
qa.a: Agreeing on regular Sunday calls, even with bad signal, gives the friendship a steady rhythm after the awkward apology.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt when Tanvir finally explained?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt relieved to know the real reason, and still a little stiff and hurt, which shows in his cautious laugh.

grounding: A lonely young adult tolerates an awkward repair after conflict and commits to regular calls with one close friend despite bad signal and distance.

passage: Madhav muted forty-two group chats on a Sunday morning in his Hyderabad flat and felt oddly lighter. He'd moved cities for work a year ago, had hundreds of followers, and still spent weekends watching other people's weddings on his phone. He picked three names instead. Shreya, from college, was the first he called. "This feels strange," he admitted. "I'm calling because I've been really lonely and I don't want to pretend I'm fine." There was a pause. Then Shreya said, "Okay. Me too, honestly." They talked for an hour about nothing and everything. He set a reminder: Shreya, every other Sunday, eleven o'clock. The first few calls were stiff; once they ran out of things to say. He kept calling anyway, and by March Shreya was the one ringing first.

qa.q: How many group chats did Madhav mute?
qa.a: Madhav muted forty-two group chats.

qa.q: How was Madhav feeling when he told Shreya the call felt strange?
qa.a: He felt awkward and exposed, but honest, admitting his loneliness instead of pretending he was fine.

qa.q: What choice kept Madhav's plan working through the stiff early calls?
qa.a: He kept calling even when they ran out of things to say, letting closeness grow from regular, honest contact.

qa.q: How did Madhav's honesty affect Shreya?
qa.a: It let Shreya admit she was lonely too, and over time she felt close enough to start ringing first.

grounding: A young adult lonely despite many contacts chooses a few people, calls regularly and is honest about struggling, and isolation eases through that openness.

passage: With the audit due Friday and half the team out sick, the Nagpur office was all ringing phones and cold chai. Irfan noticed Tanuja again: headphones on, lunch at her desk, a quick "all good!" whenever anyone asked about her weekend. She'd said no to the team dinner, the cricket match, the farewell. Irfan didn't push. On Tuesday he left a cutting chai beside her keyboard and said, "Going to the tapri at four if you want a break. No pressure." She didn't come. Wednesday, same. Thursday, at four-fifteen, she appeared at the tapri, arms crossed against the wind. They talked about the audit for ten minutes, nothing personal. As they walked back, Tanuja said, "Thanks for not asking stuff." Irfan just nodded. He planned to go again at four next week.

qa.q: What did Irfan leave beside Tanuja's keyboard on Tuesday?
qa.a: He left a cutting chai beside her keyboard.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he kept inviting Tanuja despite her silence?
qa.a: Irfan seemed quietly concerned for Tanuja and patient, not hurt by her refusals, which is why he kept the offer light.

qa.q: Why does Irfan's approach suit someone like Tanuja?
qa.a: Low-pressure invitations with no personal questions let Tanuja come on her own terms, so trust can build at her pace.

qa.q: What does Tanuja's "Thanks for not asking stuff" reveal about her experience?
qa.a: It suggests Tanuja often feels pressed to explain herself and was relieved to have company that asked for nothing.

grounding: A colleague notices someone deflecting personal questions and declining invitations, and keeps offering low-pressure tea so trust builds at her pace.

passage: Aniket had worked beside Gurleen at the Kolkata design studio for four months and still knew nothing about her beyond her coffee order. Ask about her weekend and she'd say "quiet," then ask about his. She skipped every birthday cake in the pantry. Aniket noticed she ate lunch on the fire-escape steps, alone. He didn't want to be the colleague who pries. So on Monday he said, "I walk to the lake after lunch. Join if you like, or don't." For two weeks she didn't. Then one grey Thursday she caught up with him at the gate. They walked around the lake in near-silence, watching a man feed the ducks. On the way back Gurleen said, "My mother's been unwell. I don't really talk about it." Aniket said, "Okay. Walk's there anytime." He didn't ask more.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen eat lunch?
qa.a: Gurleen ate lunch on the fire-escape steps, alone.

qa.q: What does Aniket's decision not to pry suggest he is thinking?
qa.a: Aniket seems caring but cautious, worried that pushing questions would make Gurleen withdraw further.

qa.q: How could Aniket keep supporting Gurleen after she mentioned her mother?
qa.a: He could keep offering the walk without probing, and simply listen if she brings it up again, letting her decide how much to share.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Gurleen to finally join the walk?
qa.a: It may have felt risky but relieving for Gurleen to have quiet company that didn't demand answers, enough to share one true thing.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who deflects and declines invitations, keeps offering a low-pressure walk, and lets trust build at her pace.

passage:
"Samosa?" Dilnaz held out the paper plate at the office pantry.
"No, thanks. Ate already," Mahima said, eyes on her phone.
"Okay." Dilnaz sat on the other stool anyway. "I'm going down to the bakery tomorrow at five. Their chai's terrible. You're welcome to suffer with me."
"Maybe. I've got a lot on."
"No problem."
Next day, five o'clock. Dilnaz knocked on Mahima's cabin door. "Bakery. Still terrible. Still going."
Mahima hesitated. "I really can't today."
"Sure. Same time Friday."
Friday, Mahima was already standing by the lift, bag on her shoulder. "Is it really that bad?"
"Worse," Dilnaz grinned.
Over the cracked cups, Mahima said, "I moved here after a break-up. I don't really know anyone."
Dilnaz nodded. "Well. You know the bakery now." Neither said more, and that seemed fine.

qa.q: What time does Dilnaz go to the bakery?
qa.a: Dilnaz goes to the bakery at five.

qa.q: Why does Dilnaz keep inviting Mahima after being turned down?
qa.a: Dilnaz seems to care about Mahima's loneliness and is patient, hopeful that a light, repeated offer will feel safe enough to accept.

qa.q: Which of Dilnaz's choices worked best, and why?
qa.a: Accepting each no with "No problem" and repeating the same easy invite kept pressure low, so Mahima could choose to come when she was ready.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had asked Mahima directly why she was so quiet?
qa.a: Mahima might have felt cornered and closed up, and may not have shared about her move and break-up on her own.

grounding: A colleague notices someone who turns down invitations and keeps offering low-pressure company, letting trust build at her pace.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: The bus from Aurangabad dropped Afreen and her cousin Nikita at the edge of the village just as the azaan faded. Their Nani was already at the gate, laughing, flour on her hands, asking about their exams and the neighbours' goats in one breath. Their Nana sat on the charpai inside and barely looked up. "Late," he said. "Buses in my day ran on time." All evening he grumbled about the price of fodder, the noise from the mosque loudspeaker, their Mamu who never visited. Nani hummed while rolling rotis. That night, lying on the roof under the stars, Afreen whispered, "They've lived in the same house for fifty years. How are they so different?" Nikita shrugged. Afreen stared up for a long time. "I don't want to end up like Nana," she said. "But I don't know how you choose."

qa.q: How long have Nani and Nana lived in the same house?
qa.a: They have lived in the same house for fifty years.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling when she stares up at the sky on the roof?
qa.a: Afreen feels curious and a bit uneasy, fearing she might become bitter like Nana without knowing how to choose otherwise.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to do with her question?
qa.a: Afreen could keep watching and ask Nani how she stays cheerful, and gently ask Nana about his life too, rather than deciding who he is.

qa.q: How might Nana see the girls' visit?
qa.a: Nana may feel neglected and irritable, noticing what is missing, like his son not visiting, even while the girls are right there.

grounding: A teenager sees a cheerful and a bitter grandparent side by side and wonders which path she will take, without yet grasping how choices build up.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: In Istanbul, Elif spent the spring holiday shuttling between her two grandmothers. Anneanne lived by the ferry dock and fed the gulls every morning, chatting to fishermen, forgetting her keys and laughing about it. Babaanne lived three streets up, curtains always half-drawn, listing who had wronged her: a sister, a landlord, the government, even Elif's father. Both were widows, both nearly eighty. On the ferry home, Elif's younger sister Leila asked, "Which one do you like more?" Elif didn't answer. She was thinking of how she'd sulked for three days after losing the class election, and how she had kept a list, too, of people who hadn't voted for her. "Leila," she said at last, "do you think people decide to be like that? Or it just happens?" Leila shrugged and pointed at a dolphin.

qa.q: What did Anneanne do every morning?
qa.a: Anneanne fed the gulls every morning.

qa.q: What is Elif feeling as she remembers her list after the class election?
qa.a: Elif feels uneasy and a little ashamed, recognising a small version of Babaanne's grudges in herself.

qa.q: What small step could Elif take with what she noticed?
qa.a: Elif could try letting go of her election grudge on purpose, testing whether she can choose something closer to Anneanne's lightness.

qa.q: How might Leila see the two grandmothers differently from Elif?
qa.a: Leila seems to see them as simply nicer or less nice, and hasn't yet started worrying about who she will become.

grounding: A teenager compares a contented grandmother and a bitter one and wonders which path she is on, a question she cannot yet fully answer.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: Irawati, you've been staring at that form for an hour. Let me tell you about me at twenty. I'm Tejas; your mother calls me Kaka because I'm her father's younger brother. In second year I sat by the Pune canal one night and imagined myself at sixty: a clerk in a job I'd never questioned, never having told my father I loved his old songs. That picture terrified me. First I made it worse. I rewrote my college essays twelve times, sure one wrong word would waste my life. I stopped sleeping. Then one Sunday I just went to my father's room and asked him to sing. He did, off-key. I cried. That didn't fix my career. But I stopped waiting to be perfect before being honest. So fill the form, Irawati, and call your Baba tonight.

qa.q: How many times did Tejas rewrite the college essays?
qa.a: Tejas rewrote the college essays twelve times.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when imagining being sixty by the canal?
qa.a: Tejas was terrified, fearing a life of regret in an unquestioned job with words never said to his father.

qa.q: Why was asking his father to sing a turning point in Tejas's story?
qa.a: It turned the fear into an honest act now, instead of more perfectionist rewriting, showing him he could live closer to his values without waiting.

qa.q: How might Tejas's father have felt when asked to sing?
qa.a: He was likely surprised and moved, perhaps touched that his son valued his old songs enough to ask.

grounding: An elder recalls imagining a regretful old age at twenty, first freezing into perfectionism and then choosing to act honestly now.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: The power had been out in the hostel for two hours, and Kiran's laptop was on eight percent. The scholarship statement was due at midnight. Kiran had written the first line forty times. Every version sounded like someone who'd pick a safe bank job, stop painting, and at sixty look back on nothing. The thought made Kiran's hands go cold. "Just send the third draft," Ojas said from the other bunk, by torchlight. "It was good." "Good isn't enough. What if this is the moment that decides everything?" Ojas put the torch down. "Kiran. You're going to miss the deadline being perfect." Silence. Kiran looked at the battery icon, then opened the third draft, changed one sentence to mention the painting, and pressed submit at 11:41. Then, still shaking, Kiran texted home: "I want to talk about art school this weekend."

qa.q: At what time did Kiran press submit?
qa.a: Kiran pressed submit at 11:41.

qa.q: What was Kiran afraid of while rewriting the first line?
qa.a: Kiran was afraid of ending up at sixty with regrets after a safe job, and that fear made each draft feel like it would decide everything.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The fear pushed Kiran into perfectionism that nearly cost the deadline; Ojas's blunt reminder helped Kiran submit and then take an honest step by texting home.

qa.q: How does Ojas see Kiran's struggle?
qa.a: Ojas sees the danger of chasing perfect and cares enough to speak plainly, worried Kiran will lose a real chance to an imagined one.

grounding: A student's fear of a regretful life pushes toward paralysing perfectionism before tipping into a more honest step now, amid a power cut and a deadline.

subtopic: Integrity vs despair (as foreseen by the young)
passage: After the neighbour's funeral, Eshaan couldn't stop thinking about what Mr Rao's son had said at the gate: "He always meant to take Ma to Goa. He always meant to." Back in their Chennai flat, Eshaan lay on the sofa and pictured himself at sixty, still in the accounts job Appa had chosen, still never having told Appa how much he admired him. The picture made his stomach twist. His sister Disha found him there. "You okay?" "What if I waste my life being careful?" he said. Disha sat on the arm of the sofa. "So don't. Start small." That evening Eshaan made filter coffee for Appa, sat beside him and said, "I don't say it, but I'm proud of how you raised us." Appa looked startled, then patted his knee. The job question could wait a week. This couldn't.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao's son say at the gate?
qa.a: He said, "He always meant to take Ma to Goa. He always meant to."

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel picturing himself at sixty?
qa.a: Eshaan felt anxious and afraid, his stomach twisting at the thought of a careful life full of things left unsaid.

qa.q: What was wise about Eshaan's first step?
qa.a: He acted on the fear by saying something true to Appa now, a small, honest step, instead of freezing over the bigger job question.

qa.q: What is it like for Appa to hear Eshaan's words?
qa.a: Appa is startled, then warmly touched, patting Eshaan's knee at praise he didn't expect.

grounding: A student imagines a regretful life at sixty and uses the fear to act more honestly now rather than freezing.
